_doc: How this framework spells the agnostic vocabulary. The canon — which axes exist, their canonical values, the anti-synonym glossary — lives in @ds/contracts/prop-canon.json and is framework-free. This file holds ONLY the places Vue's idiom differs from it.
_why: A contract says a component has a selection that can be controlled. It does not say whether that is `value` + `onValueChange`, `modelValue` + `update:modelValue`, or a two-way binding, because that is a framework's business and not the specification's. This file is the second half of that sentence finally being written down: the React table said `modelValue` as a hypothetical, and this is the real one.

conventions.propCase: camelCase in script, kebab-case in templates. Vue normalises the two, so the canon needs no mapping — a `readOnly` prop is written `read-only` in a template and is the same prop.
conventions.eventPrefix: update: for a model, none otherwise. Vue has no `on` prefix on the DECLARING side; `@` or `v-on` is the consumer's spelling.
conventions.booleanNaming: bare adjective, as the canon requires. Vue needs no deviation.

_controlRulesDoc: How Vue spells each `control` value from a contract's `states`. THESE ARE RULES, NOT A TABLE: one entry per control value covers every state in the library. `X` is the state name in camelCase.

consumer.note: One input, declared with defineProps. Identical to React, because there is nothing two-way about a value the user cannot change. e.g. a state named `disabled` becomes `disabled?: boolean`.

shared.note: ONE declaration, where React needs three props. `defineModel` declares the `X` prop and the `update:X` event together and returns a writable ref, so a consumer writes `v-model:X` to control it, passes `:X` alone to seed it, or passes nothing and lets the component own it. React's `defaultX` exists only because React has no two-way binding: it is a workaround for a missing language feature, not a fact about the state. THIS IS THE CLEAREST EVIDENCE THE CONTRACT STAYED AGNOSTIC — `control: shared` says WHO MAY SET IT, and the two backends spend one prop and three props saying the same thing.

internal.note: NO public input. The state still reaches CSS — as a native pseudo-class where the platform owns one, otherwise as a data attribute — but nothing outside can set it. Identical to React, and for the same reason.

_nonBooleanNote: The rules above are written for boolean states because most states drafted so far are one. An enumerated state (Checkbox's unchecked/mixed/checked) and a numeric one (Slider's value) take the same single `defineModel` with their own type, which is exactly the collapse the boolean case shows.
_slotsDoc: A contract's `composition.slots` is the one place Vue's surface is not merely a smaller version of React's — it is a DIFFERENT KIND of thing. React makes a named slot a prop typed `ReactNode`; Vue makes it a template slot, declared with `defineSlots` and filled with `<template #name>`. Both satisfy the contract's sentence; neither is derivable from it. The contract naming a slot rather than a prop is what makes that possible, and it was named that way before any Vue backend existed.

emits: <slot name="x" /> at the part the contract names
named.note: Rendered inside the anatomy part the contract names, exactly as React renders the prop there.

_axisOverridesDoc: Axis name -> the Vue prop that carries it, for the rare case where the canonical name collides with a reserved or conventional Vue prop. Empty means every axis is spelled exactly as the canon spells it, which is the desired state. Every entry needs a reason: a rename with no reason is drift with paperwork.
_behaviorBindingDoc: Behaviour vocabulary primitive -> the Vue implementation that satisfies it. The vocabulary is still unbuilt; the primitives are not, and these three are what a contract's `dismisses`, `collection.navigation` and `range` blocks compile to.
_whatVueSuppliesThatReactDoesNot: Recorded here because each one is a React binding field with no Vue counterpart, and a reader comparing the two directories will otherwise read the absence as an omission.

suppliedByTheFramework.className passthrough: Vue merges a consumer's `class` onto the root element through attribute fallthrough. React's binding has to name the node it lands on; Vue's cannot, because there is nothing to choose.
suppliedByTheFramework.ref forwarding: Vue exposes a single-root component's element as `$el`. React has no equivalent, which is what `refTarget` exists to record.
suppliedByTheFramework.event handler composition: Composed explicitly by the emitter anyway. Vue's `mergeProps` does concatenate `onX` handlers, but the emitted component turns attribute fallthrough OFF to keep identity attributes un-overridable, and that turns the automatic merge off with it. So the emitter writes the same consumer-first chain the React emitter writes — see emit/README.md.
